name: AVERAGE

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives the average (mean) of some numbers: their total divided by how many there are.

example.why: (120 + 80 + 150 + 90) / 4 = 110. Words and empty cells are left out.

notes: AVERAGEA also counts TRUE, FALSE and text in cells. MEDIAN gives the middle value instead.

name: AVERAGEA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Gives the average of some values, counting text in cells as 0, TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0.

example.why: "absent" counts as 0, so (8 + 0 + 10) / 3 = 6; AVERAGE would give 9.

notes: Empty cells are still left out.

name: AVERAGEIF

args.name: range
args.about: the cells to test

args.name: criteria
args.about: the test, like "Apple" or ">10"

args.name: average_range
args.about: the cells to average (the tested cells if left out)

about: Gives the average of the numbers in rows that pass a test.

example.why: Only the Apple rows count: (3 + 7) / 2 = 5.

notes: AVERAGEIFS takes more than one test. Gives #DIV/0! when no row passes.

name: AVERAGEIFS

args.name: average_range
args.about: the cells to average

args.name: criteria_range1
args.about: the cells for the first test

args.name: criteria1
args.about: the first test, like "North" or ">10"

args.name: criteria_range2
args.about: the cells for the next test

args.name: criteria2
args.about: the next test

about: Gives the average of the numbers in rows that pass every test.

example.why: Two rows are North and Apple: (4 + 8) / 2 = 6.

notes: The cells to average come first here, but last in AVERAGEIF.

name: COUNT

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Counts how many cells hold numbers (dates count too).

example.why: Only 34 and 29 are numbers; the word and the empty cell are not counted.

notes: COUNTA counts every cell that isn't empty.

name: COUNTA

args.name: value1
args.about: a value, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: value2
args.about: more values, cells or ranges

about: Counts how many cells are not empty, whatever they hold.

example.why: 34, "unknown" and 29 are counted; Dan's empty cell is not.

notes: COUNT counts only numbers; COUNTBLANK counts the empty cells.

name: COUNTBLANK

args.name: range
args.about: the cells to look at

about: Counts how many cells in a range are empty.

example.why: Pack and Send have no date yet.

notes: A formula that shows "" counts as empty too.

name: COUNTIF

args.name: range
args.about: the cells to test

args.name: criteria
args.about: the test, like "Apple", ">10" or "<>"

about: Counts the cells that pass a test.

example.why: 5 and 12 are more than 4.

notes: Tests can use * for any letters and ? for one letter, like "A*". COUNTIFS takes more than one test.

name: COUNTIFS

args.name: criteria_range1
args.about: the cells for the first test

args.name: criteria1
args.about: the first test, like "North" or ">10"

args.name: criteria_range2
args.about: the cells for the next test

args.name: criteria2
args.about: the next test

about: Counts the rows that pass every test.

example.why: Two North rows sold more than 10: 12 and 15.

name: MAXIFS

args.name: max_range
args.about: the cells to take the largest from

args.name: criteria_range1
args.about: the cells for the first test

args.name: criteria1
args.about: the first test

args.name: criteria_range2
args.about: the cells for the next test

args.name: criteria2
args.about: the next test

about: Gives the largest number in rows that pass every test.

example.why: Of the North rows (4, 12, 7) the largest is 12.

notes: Gives 0 when no row passes.

name: MINIFS

args.name: min_range
args.about: the cells to take the smallest from

args.name: criteria_range1
args.about: the cells for the first test

args.name: criteria1
args.about: the first test

args.name: criteria_range2
args.about: the cells for the next test

args.name: criteria2
args.about: the next test

about: Gives the smallest number in rows that pass every test.

example.why: Of the North rows (4, 12, 7) the smallest is 4.

notes: Gives 0 when no row passes.

name: GEOMEAN

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives the geometric mean: the typical rate when numbers multiply together, like yearly growth.

example.why: The cube root of 1.1 × 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.98: growing by about 25.6% every year gives the same total.

notes: All numbers must be more than 0, or it gives #NUM!.

name: FREQUENCY

args.name: data_array
args.about: the numbers to sort into groups

args.name: bins_array
args.about: the top of each group, smallest first

about: Counts how many numbers fall into each group (bin), like a histogram.

example.why: 45 is the only score up to 50; below it spill 2 (51–70), 2 (71–90) and 1 (over 90).

notes: It always gives one more cell than there are bins, for the numbers above the last one.

name: GROWTH

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values you know, which grow by a steady rate

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the steps they belong to, like 1, 2, 3

args.name: new_x's
args.about: the steps to predict for

args.name: const
args.about: FALSE to force the curve through 1 at step 0

about: Predicts values on a curve that grows by the same percentage each step.

example.why: Users double every month, so month 4 should have 800.

notes: TREND does the same for a straight line.

name: AVEDEV

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives how far the numbers are from their average, on average.

example.why: The average is 11; the numbers are 1, 3, 1 and 3 away from it, which averages 2.

notes: STDEV.S is the more common measure of spread.

name: BETA.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value, usually between 0 and 1

args.name: alpha
args.about: the first shape number, more than 0

args.name: beta
args.about: the second shape number, more than 0

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the height of the curve at x

args.name: A
args.about: the lowest possible value (0 if left out)

args.name: B
args.about: the highest possible value (1 if left out)

about: Gives the beta distribution, often used for chances and proportions that lie between 0 and 1.

example.why: With shapes 2 and 3 (values centred near 0.33), 52.48% of the curve lies below 0.4.

notes: BETA.INV goes the other way.

name: BETA.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: alpha
args.about: the first shape number

args.name: beta
args.about: the second shape number

args.name: A
args.about: the lowest possible value (0 if left out)

args.name: B
args.about: the highest possible value (1 if left out)

about: Gives the value below which a given share of a beta distribution lies (the reverse of BETA.DIST).

example.why: It undoes BETA.DIST(0.4,2,3,TRUE), which gives 0.5248.

name: BINOM.DIST

args.name: number_s
args.about: how many successes

args.name: trials
args.about: how many tries

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success in each try

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to that many, FALSE for exactly that many

about: Gives the chance of a number of successes in a fixed number of tries, like heads in coin tosses.

example.why: There are 120 ways to get exactly 3 heads among 1,024 equally likely results: 120 / 1024.

name: BINOM.DIST.RANGE

args.name: trials
args.about: how many tries

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success in each try

args.name: number_s
args.about: the fewest successes

args.name: number_s2
args.about: the most successes (just number_s if left out)

about: Gives the chance that the number of successes falls between two numbers.

example.why: Getting 4, 5 or 6 heads in 10 fair tosses happens 672 times in 1,024.

name: BINOM.INV

args.name: trials
args.about: how many tries

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success in each try

args.name: alpha
args.about: the target chance, between 0 and 1

about: Gives the smallest number of successes whose chance of being reached or undershot is at least the target.

example.why: With 100 parts each 5% likely to be faulty, there is at least a 95% chance of 9 or fewer faulty ones.

name: CHISQ.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value, 0 or more

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom: usually one less than the number of groups

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the height of the curve

about: Gives the chi-squared distribution (left tail), used to see how well counts fit what was expected.

example.why: With 1 degree of freedom, about 95% of results are below 3.84.

notes: CHISQ.DIST.RT gives the right tail, which is the one usually used in tests.

name: CHISQ.DIST.RT

args.name: x
args.about: the value, 0 or more

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom

about: Gives the chance of a chi-squared value this large or larger: small means the counts don't fit what was expected.

example.why: With 1 degree of freedom, a value of 3.84 or more happens only about 5% of the time.

name: CHISQ.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom

about: Gives the chi-squared value below which a given share of results lies (the reverse of CHISQ.DIST).

example.why: 95% of chi-squared results with 1 degree of freedom are below about 3.84.

name: CHISQ.INV.RT

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance in the right tail, between 0 and 1

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom

about: Gives the chi-squared value that is exceeded with a given chance: the cut-off for a test.

example.why: With 2 degrees of freedom, only 5% of results go above about 5.99.

name: CHISQ.TEST

args.name: actual_range
args.about: the counts you saw

args.name: expected_range
args.about: the counts you expected, same shape

about: Gives the chance that counts this far from what was expected happen by luck alone. Small means the difference is real.

example.why: Sales of four flavours were 30, 20, 25 and 25 against 25 each; a gap like that happens by luck about 57% of the time, so it proves nothing.

name: CONFIDENCE.NORM

args.name: alpha
args.about: how much doubt you accept, like 0.05 for 95% confidence

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out the values are

args.name: size
args.about: how many values were measured

about: Gives the margin of error (the ± figure) for an average, using the normal distribution.

example.why: With 50 measurements spread by 2.5, the true average is within ± 0.69 of the measured one, with 95% confidence.

notes: CONFIDENCE.T suits small samples.

name: CONFIDENCE.T

args.name: alpha
args.about: how much doubt you accept, like 0.05 for 95% confidence

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out the values are

args.name: size
args.about: how many values were measured

about: Gives the margin of error (the ± figure) for an average, using the t distribution, which suits small samples.

example.why: With only 10 measurements spread by 2.5, the true average is within ± 1.79 of the measured one, with 95% confidence.

name: COVARIANCE.P

args.name: array1
args.about: the first set of numbers

args.name: array2
args.about: the second set, the same size

about: Gives the covariance of a whole population: positive when two things tend to rise together, negative when one falls as the other rises.

example.why: Warmer days go with more ice creams sold, so it's positive (40.25).

notes: COVARIANCE.S is for a sample. CORREL gives the same idea on a scale from -1 to 1.

name: COVARIANCE.S

args.name: array1
args.about: the first set of numbers

args.name: array2
args.about: the second set, the same size

about: Gives the covariance of a sample: positive when two things tend to rise together, negative when one falls as the other rises.

example.why: Like COVARIANCE.P but divides by one less than the count, as is right for a sample.

name: DEVSQ

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Adds up the squares of how far each number is from the average.

example.why: The average is 11; 1² + 3² + 1² + 3² = 20.

name: EXPON.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value, like a waiting time

args.name: lambda
args.about: how often it happens on average, per unit

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the height of the curve

about: Gives the exponential distribution: for example the chance of waiting no longer than x for something that happens at random.

example.why: Buses come on average every 5 minutes (0.2 a minute); the chance of one within 5 minutes is about 63%.

name: F.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value, 0 or more

args.name: deg_freedom1
args.about: the degrees of freedom on top

args.name: deg_freedom2
args.about: the degrees of freedom below

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the height of the curve

about: Gives the F distribution (left tail), which compares how spread out two groups are.

example.why: About 83% of F values with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom are below 2.

notes: F.DIST.RT gives the right tail used in tests.

name: F.DIST.RT

args.name: x
args.about: the value, 0 or more

args.name: deg_freedom1
args.about: the degrees of freedom on top

args.name: deg_freedom2
args.about: the degrees of freedom below

about: Gives the chance of an F value this large or larger: small means two groups really differ in spread.

example.why: About 16% of F values with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom are 2 or more.

notes: F.TEST does the whole test from two lists of numbers.

name: F.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: deg_freedom1
args.about: the degrees of freedom on top

args.name: deg_freedom2
args.about: the degrees of freedom below

about: Gives the F value below which a given share of results lies (the reverse of F.DIST).

example.why: 95% of F values with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom are below about 3.33.

name: F.INV.RT

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance in the right tail, between 0 and 1

args.name: deg_freedom1
args.about: the degrees of freedom on top

args.name: deg_freedom2
args.about: the degrees of freedom below

about: Gives the F value exceeded with a given chance: the cut-off for a test.

example.why: Only 5% of F values with 5 and 10 degrees of freedom go above about 3.33.

name: F.TEST

args.name: array1
args.about: the first group of numbers

args.name: array2
args.about: the second group

about: Gives the chance that two groups are this different in spread by luck alone. Small means they really differ.

example.why: Machine B's parts vary much more than A's; a gap that big happens by luck only about 3% of the time.

notes: The chance covers a gap either way (two-tailed).

name: FISHER

args.name: x
args.about: a correlation, between -1 and 1 (not either end)

about: Gives the Fisher transformation of a correlation, which turns it into a number that is roughly normally spread.

example.why: It is half the natural log of (1 + 0.75) / (1 − 0.75).

notes: FISHERINV undoes it.

name: FISHERINV

args.name: y
args.about: the transformed value

about: Undoes FISHER, turning the value back into a correlation between -1 and 1.

example.why: It gives back the correlation 0.75 that FISHER turned into 0.973.

name: FORECAST

args.name: x
args.about: the point to predict for

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values you know

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the points they belong to

about: Predicts a value on the straight line that best fits the data.

example.why: Sales rise by 20 a month, so month 5 should bring 180.

notes: Older name: use FORECAST.LINEAR, which works the same.

name: FORECAST.LINEAR

args.name: x
args.about: the point to predict for

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values you know

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the points they belong to

about: Predicts a value on the straight line that best fits the data.

example.why: The best line rises by 19 a month from 82.5, so month 5 gives 82.5 + 5 × 19.

name: FORECAST.ETS

args.name: target_date
args.about: the date or point to predict for

args.name: values
args.about: the values you know

args.name: timeline
args.about: their dates or points, evenly spaced

args.name: seasonality
args.about: the length of a repeating pattern (found by itself if left out, 0 for none)

args.name: data_completion
args.about: 1 to fill gaps, 0 to treat them as zero

args.name: aggregation
args.about: how to combine values on the same date

about: Predicts a future value from a time series, using exponential smoothing that can follow trends and repeating seasons.

example.why: Sales rise by 10 every month, so September should bring 180, but Calc does not work this out yet.

notes: Not yet implemented in Calc: it always gives #N/IMPL!. For a straight-line trend use FORECAST.LINEAR or TREND.

name: FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT

args.name: target_date
args.about: the date or point to predict for

args.name: values
args.about: the values you know

args.name: timeline
args.about: their dates or points, evenly spaced

args.name: confidence_level
args.about: how sure to be, like 0.95 (the default)

args.name: seasonality
args.about: the length of a repeating pattern (found by itself if left out, 0 for none)

args.name: data_completion
args.about: 1 to fill gaps, 0 to treat them as zero

args.name: aggregation
args.about: how to combine values on the same date

about: Gives the ± margin around a FORECAST.ETS prediction for a given confidence.

example.why: The sales follow the trend exactly, so the margin should be close to 0, but Calc does not work this out yet.

notes: Not yet implemented in Calc: it always gives #N/IMPL!. For a straight-line trend use FORECAST.LINEAR or TREND.

name: FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY

args.name: values
args.about: the values you know

args.name: timeline
args.about: their dates or points, evenly spaced

args.name: data_completion
args.about: 1 to fill gaps, 0 to treat them as zero

args.name: aggregation
args.about: how to combine values on the same date

about: Gives the length of the repeating pattern that FORECAST.ETS finds in a time series.

example.why: Sales repeat 10, 20, 30, 40, so the pattern is 4 quarters long, but Calc does not work this out yet.

notes: Not yet implemented in Calc: it always gives #N/IMPL!. For a straight-line trend use FORECAST.LINEAR or TREND.

name: FORECAST.ETS.STAT

args.name: values
args.about: the values you know

args.name: timeline
args.about: their dates or points, evenly spaced

args.name: statistic_type
args.about: which figure: 1 alpha, 2 beta, 3 gamma, 4 MASE, 5 SMAPE, 6 MAE, 7 RMSE, 8 step size

args.name: seasonality
args.about: the length of a repeating pattern (found by itself if left out, 0 for none)

args.name: data_completion
args.about: 1 to fill gaps, 0 to treat them as zero

args.name: aggregation
args.about: how to combine values on the same date

about: Gives one of the figures behind a FORECAST.ETS prediction, like how strongly it smooths or how big its errors were.

example.why: 8 asks for the step size, which should be one month, but Calc does not work this out yet.

notes: Not yet implemented in Calc: it always gives #N/IMPL!. For a straight-line trend use FORECAST.LINEAR or TREND.

name: GAMMA

args.name: number
args.about: the number

about: Gives the gamma function, which extends factorials to numbers that aren't whole.
notes: Gives #NUM! for 0 and negative whole numbers.

name: GAMMA.DIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value, 0 or more

args.name: alpha
args.about: the shape number

args.name: beta
args.about: the scale number

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the height of the curve

about: Gives the gamma distribution, often used for waiting times and amounts that can't be negative.

example.why: With shape 2 and scale 2, about 59% of the waiting times are 4 hours or less.

name: GAMMA.INV

args.name: probability
args.about: the chance, between 0 and 1

args.name: alpha
args.about: the shape number

args.name: beta
args.about: the scale number

about: Gives the value below which a given share of a gamma distribution lies (the reverse of GAMMA.DIST).

example.why: Three quarters of the waiting times with shape 2 and scale 2 are below about 5.39 hours.

name: GAMMALN

args.name: x
args.about: a number more than 0

about: Gives the natural log of the gamma function.

example.why: GAMMA(5) is 24, and ln 24 ≈ 3.178.

notes: Newer name: GAMMALN.PRECISE, which works the same.

name: GAMMALN.PRECISE

args.name: x
args.about: a number more than 0

about: Gives the natural log of the gamma function.

name: GAUSS

args.name: z
args.about: how many standard deviations above the average

about: Gives the chance that a normally spread value lands between the average and z standard deviations above it.

example.why: About 34% of values lie between the average and one standard deviation above it.

notes: It is NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) − 0.5.

name: HARMEAN

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives the harmonic mean: the right average for rates, like speeds over the same distance.

example.why: Driving the same distance at 60 and then 40 km/h averages 48 km/h, not 50.

notes: All numbers must be more than 0, or it gives #NUM!.

name: HYPGEOM.DIST

args.name: sample_s
args.about: how many successes in the sample

args.name: number_sample
args.about: how many are drawn

args.name: population_s
args.about: how many successes there are in all

args.name: number_pop
args.about: how many there are in all

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to that many, FALSE for exactly that many

about: Gives the chance of a number of successes when drawing without putting back, like picking cards.

example.why: Dealing 5 cards from a pack, the chance of exactly 2 red ones is about 32.5%.

name: KURT

args.name: number1
args.about: a number, a cell or a range of cells

args.name: number2
args.about: more numbers, cells or ranges

about: Gives the kurtosis: positive when the data has more extreme values than a normal bell curve, negative when it is flatter.

example.why: Saturday's 12 is far from the others, so the data has a heavy tail and the result is well above 0.

notes: Needs at least 4 numbers.

name: LARGE

args.name: array
args.about: the numbers

args.name: k
args.about: which place: 1 for the largest, 2 for the second largest…

about: Gives the k-th largest number.

example.why: 57 is the largest, 51 the second largest.

notes: SMALL counts from the bottom.

name: LINEST

args.name: known_y's
args.about: the values you know

args.name: known_x's
args.about: the points they belong to

args.name: const
args.about: FALSE to force the line through 0

args.name: stats
args.about: TRUE for extra figures about the fit

about: Gives the slope and starting value of the straight line that best fits the data.

example.why: Each extra ad brings 2 more sales; the 10 sales without ads spill into the next cell.

notes: SLOPE and INTERCEPT give these one at a time.
